video.title: The Pure-Dextral Pinpoint | Serve Like Jakob Mensik

classification.reason: The coach explicitly instructs right-handed, right-eye dominant players to try the pure-dextral pinpoint stance and actively stretch the tossing arm up, right, and back to coil the trunk.

problem.title_as_question: How can right-handed, right-eye dominant players coil and power their serve without losing sight of the court?
problem.definition: Pure-dextral (right-handed and right-eye dominant) players struggle to create shoulder-hip coil on the serve because turning their hips back makes their dominant back eye lose peripheral vision of the court, or over-relying on spinal extension hurts their back.
problem.target_player: Right-handed, right-eye dominant tennis players struggling with serve coil, aiming, or back pain.

quotes.text: Watch where Yakob Mensic places his back foot during his pinpoint preparation. He places it on the hitting side of his off foot.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: I call this the pure dextral pinpoint because this is a common way that right-handed right eye dominant players serve.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Your accuracy is going to dramatically increase if you can see your target in peripheral vision.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: For players like Yakabmen who are right-handed and right eye dominant, that dominant eye is in the back during this preparation part of the serve.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Roger Federer's chest would probably be facing the camera, but Yakob Menick can't turn that far. He's only facing the side because that eye that's farther from the court needs that peripheral sight line.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: There are three planes of spinal motion. The first is rotation and it is the twisting action of the trunk.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: In order to get that twisting you need to stretch the off arm against the hitting hip.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: still facing forward enough. If this foot were all the way back here, then the hips are now more rotated. And in order to stretch the upper part of the trunk against the hips, you would now have to turn

quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: If you stretch the left arm this way, then it is naturally going to pull left, down, and forward when you serve, which is exactly where you want it to go.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Try the purodexual pinpoint. It'll keep your hips more forward. It'll allow you to recruit this highly useful left arm across, back, and up stretch, which will help you springload that trunk and fire into that upwards rotation.

symptoms.description: Right eye loses peripheral sight line of the target or court during serve preparation when attempting to turn chest far back.
Back foot is placed far behind the off foot in pinpoint stance, excessively turning the hips away from the court.
Server feels discomfort or strain in the back due to heavy reliance on thoracic backward extension rather than trunk rotation.

causes.statement: For right-handed right-eye dominant players, the dominant eye is located in the back during preparation and must maintain a peripheral sight line of the court, restricting how far the head and chest can turn back.
Trunk rotation power requires creating a diagonal stretch by pulling the off-arm shoulder against the hitting hip.

Placing the back foot far behind the front foot in pinpoint rotates the hips away from the court, forcing the player to turn their upper body too far back to create coil, which cuts off dominant eye vision.
Generating serve power primarily through sagittal plane thoracic backward extension rather than transverse plane rotation can overload and hurt the spine.

angles.summary: Explains the three planes of spinal motion (transverse rotation, sagittal extension/flexion, and frontal side-bending) that springload the trunk on the serve.
Contrasts Federer's closed chest rotation with pure-dextral pinpoint servers like Mensik, Watanuki, and Griekspoor whose back foot slides to the hitting side.
Analyzes Zverev's extreme thoracic backward extension spring and notes it can cause back stress for players who cannot tolerate it.
Refutes the notion that the tossing arm is only used to toss the ball, explaining it is actively used as leverage to prep and stretch the trunk.

solutions.summary: After tossing, actively drive the tossing arm up, right, and back across the body to leverage trunk coil.
solutions.external_goal: Stretch tossing arm up, to the right, and back across the body after releasing the ball

solutions.summary: Adopt the pure-dextral pinpoint stance by bringing the back foot to the hitting side of the front foot rather than behind it, keeping hips open while stretching the tossing arm.
solutions.external_goal: Bring the back foot to the hitting side of the lead foot during pinpoint slide

solutions.summary: Power the serve using transverse plane trunk rotation via the across-body arm pull rather than stressing the back with deep backward thoracic bending.
